sections.section_title: The Pāśupata Doctrine and the Fundamental Triad
sections.content: This section introduces the Pāśupata doctrine, summarized in five topics: (i) kārya (the individual soul as effect/paśu), (ii) kāraṇa (God as cause/pati), (iii) yoga (spiritual technique), (iv) vidhi (righteous conduct), and (v) duḥkhānta (final cessation of sorrow). It emphasizes that liberation is achieved solely through the grace (karuṇā) of Śiva (Rudra), not by wisdom or action, but through self-surrender (ātma-pradāna). This doctrine, articulated in texts like the Vāyavīya-saṁhitā, establishes the fundamental triad of Śaivism: paśu (the individual soul), pāśa (bondage), and pati (the lord, Śiva). It also introduces the concept of bondage (pāśa) as threefold: mala (stains/ignorance), māyā (projection/illusion), and karma (actions). The section notes that the early Āgamas, which form the scriptural basis, are primarily dualistic (dvaita) in outlook and are central to schools like Śaiva-siddhānta.
sections.summary: Introduces the five core tenets of the Pāśupata doctrine, highlighting liberation through Śiva's grace. It defines the foundational Śaiva triad of Pati (God), Paśu (soul), and Pāśa (bondage), and describes the dualistic nature of the early Śaiva Āgamas.
key_concepts: Five Fundamental Topics (kārya, kāraṇa, yoga, vidhi, duḥkhānta)

sections.section_title: The Rise of Non-Dualistic Kāśmir Śaivism
sections.content: This section details the emergence of Kāśmir Śaivism as a counter-movement to the dualism of the Āgamas. It credits Vasugupta (c. 825 A.D.) with popularizing the non-dualistic Śiva-sūtra, leading to the formation of the 'Spanda-śāstra'. This was followed by the 'Pratyabhijñā-śāstra' (doctrine of recognition), founded by Somānanda (c. 900 A.D.) and brilliantly articulated by the polymath Abhinavagupta (late 10th c. A.D.). This school posits that salvation (mokṣa) is the recognition (pratyabhijñā) of one's own divine nature (svarūpa). Despite its staunch non-dualism, Abhinavagupta claimed his philosophy was based on the 64 non-dualistic Bhairava Āgamas, distinguishing them from the dualistic Śiva Āgamas and the mixed Rudra Āgamas. The section highlights the shift from a path of devotion (bhakti) to a path of wisdom (jñāna).
sections.summary: Explains the development of non-dualistic Kāśmir Śaivism through the Spanda and Pratyabhijñā schools, founded by Vasugupta and Somānanda respectively. This tradition, emphasizing the path of wisdom (jñāna), contrasts with the dualistic, devotion-based Āgamic schools.

sections.section_title: The Codification and Supremacy of Śaiva-Siddhānta
sections.content: This section focuses on the dualistic Āgama tradition that was codified under the name 'Śaiva-siddhānta'. This school asserts its supreme authority and consistency with the Vedas, with some texts claiming the Āgama is the very essence of the Veda. The Suprabheda-āgama classifies Śaiva scriptures into four groups (Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, Miśra, Siddhānta) and declares Siddhānta as the only 'pure Śaiva' tradition, dismissing the others. The credit for establishing the importance of Siddhānta is given to teachers like Sadyojyoti (9th c. A.D.) and later Aghora-śiva (c. 1158 A.D.), who defended its dualistic position. The school holds that Śiva is the only reliable authority and that the 28 Siddhānta Āgamas are his direct revelation, constituting his 'head', while other doctrines are lesser parts of his 'body', serving as preliminary views (pūrva-pakṣa) to be ultimately superseded by Siddhānta.
sections.summary: Details the establishment of Śaiva-siddhānta as the codified, dualistic Āgamic tradition. It emphasizes its claimed Vedic consistency and supreme authority over other Śaiva schools, presenting its 28 Āgamas as the ultimate and final revelation from Śiva.

sections.content: This section traces the historical spread of Śaiva-siddhānta from Central India to South India and discusses the rise of Vīra-śaivism in Karnataka. It details a monastic lineage in Central India starting from Kadamba-guhā-vāsi (c. 675 A.D.) that influenced royalty. The tradition was later brought to the Coḷa kingdom in South India by Emperor Rājendra I (c. 1012-1044 A.D.). However, Śaivism was already flourishing in the South through the devotional hymns of the Tamil Nayanmar saints (Appar, Sundarar, etc.) from as early as the 5th-7th centuries, which formed the Tirumurai, the Tamil counterpart to the Āgamas. The philosophical works of Meykaṇḍa-deva (13th c.) further systematized Siddhānta in the Tamil region. In Karnataka, a new sect, Vīra-śaivism, emerged, founded philosophically on Śrīkaṇṭha's commentary (c. 1122 A.D.). It was popularized by the social and religious reforms of Basava (c. 1160 A.D.) and is distinguished by unique doctrines like ṣaṭ-sthalas (six stages) and the practice of wearing a liṅga (liṅga-dhāraṇa).
sections.summary: Traces the historical spread of Śaiva-siddhānta across India and the development of regional traditions. It covers its establishment in South India through both Sanskrit lineages and the indigenous Tamil Nayanmar saints, and details the emergence of the distinct Vīra-śaivism sect in Karnataka with its unique practices and philosophy.

chapter_summary: Chapter III, 'ŚAIVISM', provides a comprehensive overview of the major schools and historical development of Śaivism, primarily through the lens of the Āgamic traditions. It begins by outlining the foundational Pāśupata doctrine with its five tenets and the core triad of Pati (God), Paśu (soul), and Pāśa (bondage). The chapter then contrasts the two major philosophical streams: the dualistic (dvaita) Śaiva-siddhānta, which emphasizes liberation through devotion (bhakti) and divine grace (karuṇā), and the non-dualistic (advaita) Kāśmir Śaivism, which advocates for liberation through wisdom (jñāna) and the recognition (pratyabhijñā) of the self's identity with Śiva. It traces the historical lineage of these schools, from the early Āgamas and the teachers who systematized them like Sadyojyoti, to the non-dualist philosophers like Vasugupta and Abhinavagupta. The chapter concludes by examining the geographical spread and regional variations of Śaivism, focusing on the flourishing of Śaiva-siddhānta in South India through the Tamil Nayanmar saints and the emergence of the distinct Vīra-śaivism sect in Karnataka, with its unique social and religious practices.
key_arguments: Śaivism is not a monolithic tradition but consists of several distinct philosophical schools, primarily divided along dualistic (Śaiva-siddhānta) and non-dualistic (Kāśmir Śaivism) lines.

The concept of liberation and the means to achieve it differ significantly between schools: Śaiva-siddhānta emphasizes divine grace and devotion, while Kāśmir Śaivism prioritizes wisdom and self-recognition.
The Śaiva Āgamas are the foundational scriptures, but their interpretation (dualistic vs. non-dualistic) is a central point of divergence among the schools.
Śaiva-siddhānta posits itself as the supreme and final revelation ('siddhānta'), consistent with the Vedas, viewing other schools as preliminary steps ('pūrva-pakṣa').

The historical development of Śaivism involved a dynamic interaction between Sanskrit-based scholarly traditions and regional, vernacular devotional movements, such as the Nayanmars in Tamil Nadu and the Vīra-śaiva saints in Karnataka.
key_takeaways: The core concepts of Śaivism are the triad of Pati (Lord), Paśu (soul), and Pāśa (bondage).
The Pāśupata doctrine outlines five key areas: cause (kāraṇa), effect (kārya), spiritual practice (yoga), conduct (vidhi), and the end of suffering (duḥkhānta).
Kāśmir Śaivism, particularly the Pratyabhijñā school, is a sophisticated non-dualistic philosophy.
Śaiva-siddhānta is the dominant dualistic school, with deep roots in South India and a strong emphasis on the 28 primary Āgamas.
Vīra-śaivism (Lingayatism) is a distinct sect from Karnataka with unique theological concepts (like ṣaṭ-sthalas) and social practices (like liṅga-dhāraṇa).

historical_figures.name: Haradatta
historical_figures.significance: Author of Gaņa-kārikā, which points to the Pāśupata sect's reliance on Śaivāgamas.

historical_figures.name: Abhinava-gupta
historical_figures.significance: A major exponent of Kāśmir Śaivism and the Pratyabhijñā school. Authored key texts like Tantrāloka and Pratyabhijñā-vimarśinī. Argued for a non-dualistic interpretation of the Āgamas.
historical_figures.dates: towards the close of the tenth century A.D.

historical_figures.name: Vasugupta
historical_figures.significance: Popularized the non-dualistic Śiva-sūtra, which he is said to have discovered, laying the groundwork for Kāśmīr Śaivism.

historical_figures.name: Kallaṭa
historical_figures.significance: Propagated Vasugupta's teachings, specifically the Spanda' kārikā, and authored Spanda-Sarvasva, contributing to the Spanda-śāstra division.

historical_figures.name: Somānanda
historical_figures.significance: Authored Śiva-dṛṣṭi, the definitive text of the Pratyabhijñā school, and is hailed as the 'maker of logic' (tarkasya kartā).

historical_figures.name: Utpala
historical_figures.significance: Wrote the Kārikās on Pratyabhijñā, which helped crystallize the school's fundamental concepts.

historical_figures.name: Lakṣaṇa-gupta
historical_figures.significance: Was the student of Utpala and the teacher of the great Abhinava-gupta.

historical_figures.name: Śambhu-nātha
historical_figures.significance: A master from Jālandhara who initiated Abhinava-gupta into Āgama wisdom.

historical_figures.name: Sadyojyoti
historical_figures.significance: Credited with first using the term 'Siddhānta' for the Āgamic tradition and revealing the 'royal road' to Śiva-siddhānta. Hailed as the 'kulaguru' of the school.

historical_figures.name: Bṛhaspati
historical_figures.significance: Colleague of Sadyojyoti, also credited with establishing the Siddhānta school.

historical_figures.name: Ugra-jyoti
historical_figures.significance: Teacher of Sadyojyoti.

historical_figures.name: Rājānaka-Rāmakaṇṭha
historical_figures.significance: A scholar from Kāśmīra who wrote a commentary on Sadyojyoti's Mokṣa-kārikā.

historical_figures.name: Jayaratha
historical_figures.significance: Commentator on Abhinava-gupta's work.

historical_figures.name: Aghora-śiva
historical_figures.significance: Valiantly defended the dualistic position of all 28 Āgamas, clearly distinguishing Śaiva-siddhānta from other Śaiva schools.

historical_figures.name: Śrīkaṇṭha
historical_figures.role: Master in Sadyojyoti's lineage / Vīra-śaiva philosopher
historical_figures.significance: Two figures with the same name are mentioned. One authored Ratna-traya in the Siddhānta tradition. The other wrote a commentary on the Vedānta-sūtras (c. 1122 A.D.) which formed the philosophical basis for Vīra-śaivism.

historical_figures.name: Kadamba-guhā-vāsi
historical_figures.significance: Headed a Śaiva monastic settlement of the Siddhānta division in Central India, indicating its early presence there.

historical_figures.name: Rudra-śambhu
historical_figures.significance: Established a sanctuary in Āmardaka (Ujjayinī) and became the royal preceptor to the Kākatiya kings, spreading Siddhānta influence.

historical_figures.name: Rājendra I
historical_figures.significance: Is reported to have brought Śaiva-siddhānta teachers from North India to the Coḷa country, boosting the tradition's presence in the South.

historical_figures.name: Appar (Tiru-Nāvukkarasu)
historical_figures.significance: A key figure in the Bhakti movement in Tamil Nadu, his devotional hymns (part of the Tevāram) helped spread Śaivism among the masses.

historical_figures.name: Tiru-Jñāna-sam-bandar
historical_figures.significance: Along with Appar, he was responsible for the spread of Śaivism in the Pallava and Pāṇḍya territories through his hymns.

historical_figures.name: Sundarar
historical_figures.significance: One of the three main authors of the Tevāram hymns.

historical_figures.name: Tiru-mūlar
historical_figures.significance: Author of the Tirumantiram, an important Tamil Śaiva text. Said to have brought the 28 Āgamas to the Tamil country.

historical_figures.name: Māṇikka-vācakar
historical_figures.significance: Author of the celebrated Tiru-vācakam. The text notes a conflict in his dating.
historical_figures.dates: second or third century OR 9th century A.D.

historical_figures.name: Nambi-Āṇḍār-Nambi
historical_figures.significance: Redacted the devotional songs of the Tamil saints into the twelve books of the Tirumurai.

historical_figures.name: Meykaṇḍa-deva
historical_figures.significance: Authored the Śiva-jñāna-bodham, a foundational philosophical text of Tamil Śaiva-siddhānta.

historical_figures.name: Aruḷ-nandi-Śivācārya
historical_figures.significance: Explained and popularized the teachings of Meykaṇḍa-deva.

historical_figures.name: Umā-pati-Śivācārya
historical_figures.significance: Also explained and popularized the teachings of Meykaṇḍa-deva.

historical_figures.name: Basava
historical_figures.significance: A pivotal figure in the Vīra-śaiva movement in Karnataka.

historical_figures.name: Allama-prabhu
historical_figures.significance: Became the first leader of the 'Śūnya-siṁhāsana' (Throne of the Void), an academy of mystics in the Vīra-śaiva movement.

historical_events.significance: Represents the ancient roots of Tamil Śaiva devotionalism.
Authoring of Tirumantiram and the claimed transmission of Āgamic knowledge to the South.

historical_events.event: Reign of Pallava monarch Mahendra-varma I.
historical_events.significance: Period of the flourishing of the Bhakti movement led by saints like Appar.

historical_events.event: Activity of Nayanmar saints Appar, Tiru-Jñāna-sam-bandar, and Sundarar.
historical_events.significance: Composition of the Tevāram hymns and widespread popularization of Śaivism in the Tamil region.

historical_events.event: Leadership of Kadamba-guhā-vāsi in a Central Indian Siddhānta monastery.
historical_events.significance: Provides inscriptional evidence for the organized presence of Śaiva-siddhānta in Central India.
Marks the historical origin of Kāśmīr Śaivism as a distinct non-dualistic school.
Systematization of the Śaiva-siddhānta school and the first use of the term 'Siddhānta'.
Establishes the Pratyabhijñā school of Kāśmīr Śaivism.
The peak of Kāśmīr Śaivism's philosophical development.

historical_events.event: Reign of Coḷa emperor Rājendra I.
historical_events.significance: Facilitated the exchange of Śaiva traditions between North and South India.

historical_events.event: Śrīkaṇṭha writes his commentary on the Vedānta-sūtras.
historical_events.significance: Provided the philosophical foundation for the emerging Vīra-śaivism sect.
A major event in the Vīra-śaiva movement, creating a center for spiritual discourse and reform.
A key moment in the defense and definition of the dualistic Śaiva-siddhānta position.

historical_events.event: Activity of Basava and other Vīra-śaiva saints.
historical_events.significance: The Vīra-śaiva movement gains considerable force as a movement for religious and social reform.
Composition of Śiva-jñāna-bodham, a seminal text for Tamil Śaiva-siddhānta philosophy.

geographic_locations.context: The primary center for the development of non-dualistic Kāśmir Śaivism, including the Spanda and Pratyabhijñā schools.
geographic_locations.significance: A major hub of Śaiva philosophy and scholarship.

geographic_locations.context: A stronghold of the dualistic Śaiva-siddhānta school and the heartland of the Nayanmar bhakti movement.
geographic_locations.significance: Crucial for the development of devotional Śaivism and its vernacular literature.

geographic_locations.context: The region where Vīra-śaivism (Lingayatism) primarily prevails.
geographic_locations.significance: Home to a unique and influential Śaiva sect focused on social reform.

geographic_locations.context: Region with early medieval Śaiva monastic settlements, and the homeland of the teacher Sadyojyoti.
geographic_locations.significance: An important early center for the Siddhānta school before its major spread in the South.

geographic_locations.context: A site where Rudra-śambhu established a sanctuary and where emperor Rājendra I met with Śaiva masters.
geographic_locations.significance: An influential monastic center connecting Śaiva traditions of Central and South India.

geographic_locations.context: Described as a region where Āgama doctrines were already prevalent and where some key texts were prepared.
geographic_locations.significance: A vital region for the preservation, development, and expression of Āgamic Śaivism.

geographic_locations.context: The kingdom where Rājendra I settled Śaiva teachers from the north.
geographic_locations.significance: A key site for the patronage and growth of Śaiva-siddhānta in the medieval period.

geographic_locations.context: The city where the 'Śūnya-siṁhāsana', the spiritual assembly of the Vīra-śaivas, was established in 1156 A.D.
geographic_locations.significance: The epicenter of the Vīra-śaiva reform movement.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: The individual soul, seen as an effect of the divine cause.
A term for the individual soul, signifying its state of bondage and dependence.
God (Śiva), the ultimate cause of everything.
A term for God (Śiva) as the lord of all individual souls (paśu).
The forces that bind the soul, consisting of mala, māyā, and karma.
The discipline of mind and meditation to achieve spiritual goals.
Worldly conduct based on virtue, conducive to attaining the values of life.
The final cessation of sorrow, or liberation, caused by bondage.
The grace of Śiva, considered the sole cause of liberation in the Pāśupata and Siddhānta schools.
The act of surrendering oneself to God to obtain liberation.
The path of devotion, central to schools like Śaiva-siddhānta.
The philosophical outlook that God, soul, and world are eternally distinct realities.
The philosophical outlook that reality is ultimately one, and the soul is identical to God.
A philosophical position that attempts to reconcile dualistic and non-dualistic views.
Another name for Kāśmir Śaivism, referring to the triad of paśu, pati, and pāśa.
The primary bond (pāśa) that causes ignorance and hides the soul's true nature.
The bond (pāśa) that creates the various planes of existence and experience.
The bond (pāśa) of good and bad actions that results in phenomenal experiences.
The path of wisdom, central to Kāśmir Śaivism.
The core concept of a school of Kāśmir Śaivism, referring to the recognition of the self's divine nature.
The ultimate goal of spiritual practice.
The true, essential nature of the self, which in non-dualism is identical to Śiva.
The name for the codified dualistic Āgama tradition.
The form of Śaivism prevalent in Karnataka, also known as Lingayatism.
A key doctrine in Vīra-śaivism describing the six planes of spiritual experience.
A characteristic doctrine of Vīra-śaivism.
The mystic and direct experience of the divine presence, a key concept in Vīra-śaivism.

quotations.quote: तस्मात्पुरुषार्थकामैः पुरुषधोरेयैः पंचार्थप्रतिपादनपरं पाशुपतशास्त्रमाश्रयणीयम्।
quotations.context: Summarizing the Pāśupata doctrine's importance for achieving the four values of life.

quotations.quote: प्रसादात् स दुःखान्तः प्राप्यते, न तु ज्ञानवैराग्यधर्मैश्वर्यत्यागमात्रादित्यर्थः ।
quotations.context: Explaining that the end of sorrow (liberation) is obtained through grace alone, not by other means.

quotations.quote: रुतस्य भयस्य द्रावणात्संयोजनाद्रुद्रः ।
quotations.context: Providing an etymological definition of 'Rudra' as one who produces and eliminates fear.

quotations.quote: मलमायादिभिः पाशैः स बध्नाति पशुपतिः । स एव मोचकस्तेषां भक्त्या सम्यगुपासितः ।।
quotations.context: Stating that Paśupati (Śiva) is responsible for both binding souls with fetters and for releasing them when worshipped with devotion.

quotations.quote: पशूनां भुक्तिमुक्त्सर्थ पतिः पशुपतिः स्मृतः ।
quotations.context: Defining Paśupati as the Lord who is responsible for the worldly experience and liberation of souls (paśus).

quotations.quote: पशुः पाशः पतिश्चैव त्रिपदार्थ उदाह्यतः ।
quotations.context: Stating the three fundamental categories (tripadārtha) as paśu, pāśa, and pati.

quotations.quote: पाश्यः पाशयिता पाशास्त्रयमेतद् व्यवस्थितम्। साध्यसाधनभावोक्त्या यथावत्प्रकारं भवेत्।।
quotations.context: Explaining the triad as the bound (pāśya), the binder (pāśayitā), and the bond (pāśa).

quotations.quote: पाशा अपि त्रयो ज्ञेया मलं माया च कर्म च। ... संसारी स पशुर्बद्धो मुक्त पाशत्रयोज्झितः ॥
quotations.context: A detailed verse explaining the three bonds (mala, māyā, karma) and how the soul is bound by them and liberated when freed from them.

quotations.quote: केवलः सकलः शुद्धस्त्र्यवस्थः पुरुषः स्मृतः ।
quotations.context: Describing the three states of the soul (puruṣa) as Kevala, Sakala, and Śuddha.

quotations.quote: त्रिधा सोऽयमनुग्राह्यः सकलः प्रलयाकलः । ... मलैकसंबद्धो विज्ञानकल उच्यते ॥
quotations.context: Further explaining the three types of souls to be graced: Sakala, Pralayākala, and Vijñānakala, based on which fetters bind them.

quotations.quote: पशवस्त्रिविधा ज्ञेयाः सकलः प्रलयाकलः। ... तृतीयः पठ्यते तन्त्रे नाम्ना विज्ञानकेवलः ॥
quotations.context: Another detailed verse defining the three types of souls (paśus) based on their bondage.

quotations.quote: चतुर्विधं ज्ञेय वामदक्षिणमिश्रकम्। सिद्धान्तेन समायुक्तं चतुर्थैव प्रकीर्तितम् ।। ... शैवबाह्याः समाख्यातास्ते तु शैवेऽप्यपूजिताः ॥
quotations.context: Classifying Śaiva scriptures into four groups and declaring Siddhānta as the supreme one, while dismissing the other three as outside the Śaiva fold.

quotations.quote: याभ्यां प्रकाशितं वर्त्म सिद्धान्ते सिद्धभावतः । गुरूणामपि तौ वन्द्यौ सद्योज्योतिबृहस्पती॥
quotations.context: Praising Sadyojyoti and Bṛhaspati as the two revered masters who revealed the path of Siddhānta.

quotations.quote: आप्तोक्तिस्तु सिद्धान्तः शिव एवाप्तिमान्यतः। ... आप्तस्तु शिव एवैकः शिवान्ये त्वशिवा मताः ॥
quotations.context: Defining 'siddhānta' as the word of a reliable authority (āpta), and stating that only Śiva is that authority.

quotations.quote: आप्तोक्तिरागमः सोऽपि परोक्षार्थैकसाधनम्। ... यो वक्ति सोऽयमाप्तः स्यात्तस्मादाप्ततरः शिवाः ॥
quotations.context: Stating that the Āgama is the word of a reliable authority and the only means for knowing unseen things, and Śiva is the most reliable authority.

quotations.quote: इदं ज्ञानं सिद्धान्तं परमं शुभम् । ऊर्ध्वस्रोतोद्भवं अष्टाविशंतितन्त्रकम्॥
quotations.context: Describing the knowledge of Siddhānta as supreme and originating from the 'upper stream' of 28 tantras.

quotations.quote: शैवं पुनश्चतुर्भेदं वामदक्षिणमेव च। मिश्र चैव सिद्धान्तं तेषु सिद्धान्तमुत्तमम्॥ अष्टाविंशभेदेन सिद्धान्तं श्रुणु तत्त्वतः ॥
quotations.context: Reiterating the four divisions of Śaivism and proclaiming the 28-fold Siddhānta as the best among them.

quotations.quote: शैवं चतुर्विधं प्रोक्तं शैवं पाशुपतं तथा । ... तत्रापि शैव सिद्धान्तः सर्वेभ्यो ह्युत्तमोत्तमः ॥
quotations.context: Listing various Śaiva schools and asserting that Śaiva-siddhānta is the best of all.

quotations.quote: कामिकादि शिवज्ञानं मूर्धा भगवतः सदा । इतराणि महेशस्य हत्कण्ठाद्यंगकानि वै।
quotations.source: Not specified, but context implies a Siddhānta text
quotations.context: Claiming that the Āgamas beginning with Kāmika are the head of God, while other scriptures are lesser limbs like the heart and throat.

quotations.quote: पूर्वपक्षतया तानि कथितानीह शंभुना । हेयोपादेयवस्तूनां निर्णये परमार्थतः । तत्सर्वमधरीकृत्य शैवसिद्धान्त ईरितः ॥
quotations.context: Stating that other doctrines were revealed by Śiva only as preliminary views (pūrva-pakṣa) to be superseded by the final truth of Śaiva-siddhānta.

quotations.quote: संस्कृतैः प्राकृतैर्वाक्यैश्च शिष्यानुरूपतः । देशभाषाद्युपायैश्च बोधयेत् स गुरुः स्मृतः ॥
quotations.context: Instructing that a guru should teach disciples in whatever language is suitable, be it Sanskrit, Prakrit, or local languages.

quotations.quote: वयं तु वेदागमयोर्भेदं न पश्यामः ।
quotations.context: Declaring that 'We see no difference between the Vedas and the Āgamas'.

quotations.quote: लिंगधारणमाख्यातं द्विधा सर्वार्थसाधकम् । बाह्यमाभ्यन्तरं चेति मुनिभिर्मोक्षकांक्षिभिः॥
quotations.context: Commending the wearing of the liṅga in two forms, external (physical) and internal (mental concentration), for those seeking liberation.

controversial_points: The relationship between Āgamas and Vedas is presented with varying claims: some texts state the Āgamas are the 'essence' of the Vedas or that their prescribed conduct is 'Vedic', while other traditions see them as an independent and, in some cases, superior revelation.

The philosophical classification of certain Āgamas is contested. Abhinavagupta sees a set of 18 Āgamas as teaching 'dualism-and-non-dualism', whereas the Śaiva-siddhānta school views them as purely dualistic.
There is a direct contradiction in the text regarding the historical date of the Tamil saint Māṇikka-vācakar, who is placed in both the 2nd/3rd century (p. 42) and the 9th century (p. 43).

Abhinavagupta's claim that his non-dualistic Pratyabhijñā philosophy is based on the 64 Āgamas can be seen as a reinterpretation to grant scriptural authority to a philosophical system that differs significantly from the predominantly dualistic tone of the earlier Āgamas.
alternative_viewpoints: Dualism (Dvaita) vs. Non-dualism (Advaita): The chapter presents the fundamental philosophical divide within Śaivism. Śaiva-siddhānta holds a dualistic view of reality (God, soul, and matter are distinct), while Kāśmir Śaivism espouses a monistic view where all reality is a manifestation of Śiva.

Path of Grace/Devotion (Bhakti) vs. Path of Wisdom (Jñāna): The Pāśupata and Siddhānta traditions emphasize that liberation comes solely through divine grace, attained via devotion and surrender. In contrast, Kāśmir Śaivism advocates the path of wisdom, where liberation is the direct recognition of one's own divine nature.

Scriptural Hierarchy: The Śaiva-siddhānta school, as per the Suprabheda-āgama, dismisses other Śaiva traditions like Spanda (Vāma) and Bhairava Tantras (Dakṣiṇa) as 'outside the Śaiva fold'. This contrasts sharply with the view from Kāśmir Śaivism, where the Bhairava Tantras are considered the highest revelation.
